content: This updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2009, focuses on dietary interventions for recurrent abdominal pain (RAP) in children, including those with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). RAP is a prevalent issue, affecting 4% to 25% of school-aged children, and in most cases, no organic cause for the pain is identified through physical examination or diagnostic testing. Various dietary strategies have been proposed to alleviate RAP symptoms, including the exclusion of certain dietary components or the addition of supplements like fiber or probiotics. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of dietary interventions in reducing pain in school-aged children with RAP. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing dietary interventions to placebo or no treatment in children aged 5 to 18 years, diagnosed with RAP or functional gastrointestinal disorders based on the Rome III criteria. A total of 19 RCTs, reported in 27 publications, were included, involving 1,453 participants aged 4 to 18 years from eight countries. Most participants were recruited from pediatric gastroenterology clinics, with a mean age at recruitment ranging from 6.3 to 13.1 years. Girls were more frequently represented than boys in most trials. The studies were categorized into four groups: probiotic-based interventions (13 studies), fiber-based interventions (4 studies), low FODMAP diets (1 study), and fructose-restricted diets (1 study). Follow-up periods ranged from one to five months. Probiotic-Based Interventions: Children treated with probiotics experienced a greater reduction in pain frequency within 0 to 3 months post-intervention compared to those receiving placebo (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.98 to -0.12; 6 trials; 523 children). Pain intensity also decreased in the probiotic group during the same period (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.15; 7 studies; 575 children). However, the quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as low due to unclear risks of bias and significant heterogeneity. Probiotics were associated with a higher likelihood of pain improvement at 0 to 3 months post-intervention compared to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 1.63, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.47; 7 studies; 722 children). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 8, meaning that 8 children would need to receive probiotics for 1 to experience pain improvement. This evidence was judged to be of moderate quality due to heterogeneity. In children with IBS, probiotics were more effective in improving pain at 0 to 3 months post-intervention compared to placebo (OR 3.01, 95% CI 1.77 to 5.13; 4 studies; 344 children). Probiotics also showed benefits in pain improvement at 3 to 6 months post-intervention (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.10 to 3.43; 2 studies; 224 children). Both outcomes were supported by moderate-quality evidence, though the small sample sizes limited confidence in the findings. Fiber-Based Interventions: Fiber-based interventions did not significantly improve pain at 0 to 3 months post-intervention compared to placebo (OR 1.83, 95% CI 0.92 to 3.65; 2 studies; 136 children). There was also no significant reduction in pain intensity (SMD -1.24, 95% CI -3.41 to 0.94; 2 studies; 135 children). The evidence for these outcomes was rated as low quality due to unclear risks of bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity. Low FODMAP and Fructose-Restricted Diets: Only one study each was available for low FODMAP diets and fructose-restricted diets, preventing pooled analyses. As a result, no conclusions could be drawn regarding their effectiveness. Secondary Outcomes: The review could not perform meta-analyses for secondary outcomes such as school performance, social or psychological functioning, or quality of daily life due to insufficient data and lack of comparable measures across studies. Adverse Events: With the exception of one study, all trials monitored for adverse events, and no major adverse events were reported. Conclusions: Moderateto low-quality evidence suggests that probiotics may be effective in reducing pain in children with RAP. Clinicians may consider probiotics as part of a comprehensive management approach. However, further research is needed to assess long-term outcomes, refine estimates of effect size, and determine the optimal probiotic strain and dosage. Future studies should also investigate the efficacy of probiotics in children with varying symptom profiles, such as those with IBS. Evidence for fiber-based interventions was limited and of low quality, providing no convincing support for their effectiveness in managing RAP. High-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes are needed to evaluate the potential benefits of fiber supplements. Additional trials are required to assess the effectiveness of low FODMAP diets and other dietary interventions to enable evidence-based recommendations.
